images.caption: Figure 1.From diverse failure cases of Gaussian avatars, EDGAR learns to refine arbitrary avatars trained with a video or an image, acting as both an artifact remover and a quality enhancer.

Figure 2.Examples from EDGAR-SET and discarded samples. We filter out cases where the geometry or expression is misaligned, making the recovery target ambiguous. Samples are removed when the combination ofIfI_{f}andIrI_{r}from novel views or expressions cannot reliably reproduceIg​tI_{gt}.

Figure 3.Configuration of EDGAR-SET. The dataset is constructed under diverse conditions to capture a wide range of Gaussian avatar failure cases.The view-count groups (one, two to four, and at least five) are mutually exclusive and account for 23%, 51%, and 26% of retained examples, respectively.
Figure 4.Network architecture of EDGAR. EDGAR learns to refine rendered images of Gaussian avatars using EDGAR-SET. The fuse block in the Upblock of Diffusion UNet is simplified.
Figure 5.Avatar refinement process using EDGAR. Multi-view renderings of the source Gaussian avatar are refined by EDGAR and used as supervision targets for Gaussian avatar refinement.

Figure 6.Comparison of self-reenactment results. Our method refines each baseline by restoring facial details such as the eyes, wrinkles, and sharper hair, whereas SDEdit-based refinement alters the source identity. The upper rows show outputs from avatars trained or optimized with fewer input images or views (one image for CAP4D, one video for RGBAvatar, and eight videos for GaussianAvatars), while the lower rows show outputs from avatars trained with more images or videos.Each block uses a different identity and input severity, so comparisons are made within each reconstruction method. The more severely degraded GaussianAvatars example is improved but remains only partially corrected.

Figure 7.Comparison of cross-reenactment results rendered at novel views. Our method refines each face by restoring facial details while effectively removing Gaussian artifacts such as floating blobs. In contrast, SDEdit-based refinement introduces identity shifts and oversmoothing skin texture.

Figure 8.Matched-subject comparison at the same evaluation frame. Native inputs are four images for CAP4D, four videos for RGBAvatar, and ten videos for GaussianAvatars. Identity and evaluation frame are shared, while input regimes and initial reconstruction quality differ across pipelines.

Figure 9.Large-yaw with optional open-mouth examples for RGBAvatar with four input videos. Rows show examples with absolute yaw angles of37.4∘37.4^{\circ},37.7∘37.7^{\circ}, and36.3∘36.3^{\circ}, respectively. Examples are selected near each identity’s median ground-truth yaw and mouth opening within the combined subset.

Figure 10.Ablation study results forIrI_{r}and Synthetic data. Some of the artifacts in the hair, ears, and floating blobs exhibited by the input Gaussian avatar are mitigated by the ablated variants. Nonetheless, the variant withoutIrI_{r}produces altered details and overly smooth textures due to the absence of reference information, while the variant without synthetic data retains artifacts such as distortions around the ears and floating Gaussian blobs. In contrast, the full model better preserves identity while effectively removing artifacts and improving overall visual quality. Visible artifacts in the ear and floating Gaussian blobs are highlighted in red boxes.
Figure 11.Ablation study results onℒe​x​p\mathcal{L}_{exp}. Removingℒe​x​p\mathcal{L}_{exp}degrades the preservation of facial expression details.

Figure 12.Qualitative results for the MoE ablation. All variants reduce artifacts, but the variants without MoE and with two experts retain sharp white artifacts around the ears. The full model suppresses these artifacts more effectively in this example.
